claim: The metabolic enzyme O-GlcNAc Transferase (OGT) moonlights on the chromatin of D. melanogaster gustatory neurons to instruct changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription that underlie sensory adaptations to a high-sugar diet.
source: Here, we show that the metabolic enzyme O-GlcNAc Transferase (OGT) moonlights on the chromatin of the D. melanogaster gustatory neurons to instruct changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription that underlie sensory adaptations to a high-sugar diet.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including Dam-ID, CaTaDA, and behavioral assays shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: OGT works synergistically with the Mitogen Activated Kinase/Extracellular signal Regulated Kinase (MAPK/ERK) rolled and its effector stripe to integrate activity information.
source: OGT works synergistically with the Mitogen Activated Kinase/Extracellular signal Regulated Kinase (MAPK/ERK) rolled and its effector stripe (also known as EGR2 or Krox20) to integrate activity information.
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction experiments, motif enrichment analysis, and behavioral data showing epistatic relationships between OGT, rolled, and stripe.

claim: OGT cooperates with the epigenetic silencer Polycomb Repressive Complex 2.1 (PRC2.1) to decrease chromatin accessibility and repress transcription in the high-sugar diet.
source: OGT also cooperates with the epigenetic silencer Polycomb Repressive Complex 2.1 (PRC2.1) to decrease chromatin accessibility and repress transcription in the high-sugar diet.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-occupancy analysis, chromatin accessibility measurements, and genetic epistasis experiments showing OGT and PRC2.1 function in the same pathway.

claim: Integration of nutritional and activity information changes the taste neurons' responses to sugar and the flies' ability to sense sweetness.
source: This integration of nutritional and activity information changes the taste neurons' responses to sugar and the flies' ability to sense sweetness.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology and proboscis extension response (PER) behavioral assays showing altered sugar responses with dietary and genetic manipulations.

claim: In humans and rodents, the dietary concentration of sugars affects sweetness intensity or the electrophysiological responses of the sensory nerves to sucrose.
source: For example, in humans and rodents, the dietary concentration of sugars affects sweetness intensity or the electrophysiological responses of the sensory nerves to sucrose (Wise et al., 2016; McCluskey et al., 2020; Sung et al., 2022; Sartor et al., 2011; May and Dus, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in humans and rodents.

claim: Diets supplemented with 15–30% sucrose, glucose, or fructose decrease the responses of the sensory neurons to sucrose and the transmission of the sweetness signal to higher brain areas in flies.
source: A similar phenomenon occurs in flies, where diets supplemented with 15–30% sucrose, glucose, or fructose decrease the responses of the sensory neurons to sucrose and the transmission of the sweetness signal to higher brain areas (May et al., 2019; Vaziri et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Ganguly et al., 2021; May et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: In rats and flies, the dulling of the sensory system to sugar occurs even without weight gain, suggesting that diet exposure is sufficient to drive sweet-taste plasticity.
source: In rats and flies, the dulling of the sensory system to sugar occurs even without weight gain, suggesting that diet exposure is sufficient to drive sweet-taste plasticity (Sung et al., 2022; May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing weight-independent effects of diet on taste plasticity.

claim: Knockdown of OGT exclusively in the fly sweet-taste cells prevented the neural and behavioral decrease in sugar responses observed with a high-sugar diet.
source: Specifically, knockdown of OGT exclusively in the fly sweet-taste cells prevented the neural and behavioral decrease in sugar responses observed with a high-sugar diet (May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 3B of the current manuscript.

claim: OGT uses the metabolic end-product of the HBP, UDP-GlcNAc, to post-translationally modify proteins and change their stability or activity.
source: OGT uses the metabolic end-product of the HBP, UDP-GlcNAc, to post-translationally modify proteins and change their stability or activity (Hart, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge about OGT function.

claim: OGT activity is sensitive to all cellular levels of UDP-GlcNAc without substrate inhibition, but it is enhanced by high dietary sugar due to a higher flux through the HBP.
source: OGT activity is sensitive to all cellular levels of UDP-GlcNAc without substrate inhibition, but it is enhanced by high dietary sugar due to a higher flux through the HBP (Hanover et al., 2010; Bouché et al., 2004; Hawkins et al., 1997; Marshall et al., 2004; Wang et al., 1998; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017; May et al., 2019; Wilinski et al., 2019; Na et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies on OGT activity and HBP flux.

claim: OGT is a nucleocytoplasmic protein that interacts with many chromatin- and DNA-modifying complexes.
source: OGT is also a nucleocytoplasmic protein that interacts with many chromatin- and DNA-modifying complexes; as such, it is thought to function as a nutrigenomic sensor, bridging diet and genes (Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017; Olivier-Van Stichelen and Hanover, 2015; Hart, 2019; Hardivillé and Hart, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on OGT localization and interactions.

claim: OGT is thought to function as a nutrigenomic sensor, bridging diet and genes.
source: OGT is also a nucleocytoplasmic protein that interacts with many chromatin- and DNA-modifying complexes; as such, it is thought to function as a nutrigenomic sensor, bridging diet and genes (Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017; Olivier-Van Stichelen and Hanover, 2015; Hart, 2019; Hardivillé and Hart, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature and tested in the current study.

claim: Despite global changes in HBP flux with high dietary sugar, the consequences of OGT activity differ among cell types.
source: Despite global changes in HBP flux with high dietary sugar, the consequences of OGT activity differ among cell types.
evidence: This is an observation that motivates the study, based on established knowledge about metabolic pathways.

claim: OGT decorates nutrient-sensitive loci also occupied by the epigenetic silencer PRC2.1 and the activity-dependent ERK effector Stripe (Sr).
source: In the sensory neurons, OGT decorates nutrient-sensitive loci also occupied by the epigenetic silencer PRC2.1 and the activity-dependent ERK effector Stripe (Sr).
evidence: Supported by Dam-ID co-occupancy data and motif enrichment analysis shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: The cooperation between OGT, PRC2.1, and Stripe leads to changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription that drive sensory plasticity.
source: This cooperation leads to changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription that drive sensory plasticity, and the catalytic activity of OGT plays an instructional role in this process.
evidence: Supported by CaTaDA data, RNA-seq, and behavioral assays with genetic and pharmacological manipulations.

claim: The catalytic activity of OGT plays an instructional role in sensory plasticity.
source: This cooperation leads to changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription that drive sensory plasticity, and the catalytic activity of OGT plays an instructional role in this process.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments using catalytically dead OGT mutants and OGT inhibitor OSMI shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Dam::OGT was associated with chromatin at introns (51%) and transcriptional start sites (TSSs) and promoters (30%).
source: Dam::OGT was associated with chromatin at introns (51%) and transcriptional start sites (TSSs) and promoters (30%) (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1; all peaks)
evidence: Supported by Dam-ID data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in supplementary files.

claim: OGT chromatin association patterns in flies are similar to those observed in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: these patterns are similar to those observed in the only other study that measured OGT occupancy on the chromatin of mouse embryonic stem cells (Vella et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison to previous study in mouse cells, supported by citation.

claim: OGT was enriched in transcriptionally active yellow euchromatin (453 genes).
source: Our analysis found that OGT was enriched in transcriptionally active yellow euchromatin (453 genes), consistent with its role in splicing
evidence: Supported by chromatin domain analysis shown in Figure 1C and known role of OGT in splicing.

claim: OGT was enriched at 'blue' Polycomb heterochromatin (415 genes).
source: and at 'blue' Polycomb heterochromatin (415 genes), consistent with the known associations between Polycomb Group proteins and this metabolic enzyme (Gambetta et al., 2009; Hart, 2019; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by chromatin domain analysis shown in Figure 1C and citations to previous studies.

claim: The majority of OGT binding intervals were shared between a control diet and sugar diet.
source: Although the majority of intervals were shared between a CD and SD (Figure 1E, find_peaks False Discovery Rete (FDR) <0.01), a few hundred loci were uniquely associated with OGT in either the CD (36%) or SD (10%) only conditions.
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Chromatin accessibility at OGT-bound peaks decreased in the high-sugar diet condition.
source: However, the chromatin accessibility at OGT-bound peaks decreased in the high-sugar diet condition (Figure 1F, both at blue and yellow regions, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by CaTaDA data shown in Figure 1F and supplement.

claim: On control diet only, OGT-decorated genes were involved in signal transduction, membrane potential, and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase activity.
source: On CD only, OGT-decorated genes were involved in signal transduction, membrane potential, and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase activity (Figure 1G, left).
evidence: Supported by iPAGE pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Genes targeted by OGT in the sugar diet-only condition were enriched in G-protein-coupled receptor activity, synaptic target attraction, and transcription.
source: Instead, genes targeted by OGT in the SD-only condition were enriched in G-protein-coupled receptor activity, synaptic target attraction, and transcription (Figure 1G, left).
evidence: Supported by iPAGE pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Genes with differential OGT binding between sugar diet and control diet were enriched for regulatory/signaling and neural GO terms, including dendrite morphogenesis, neuron projection membrane, synaptic target attraction, signal transduction, pattern formation, and asymmetric cell division.
source: Finally, genes with differential OGT binding between SD/CD were enriched for regulatory/signaling and neural GO terms, including dendrite morphogenesis, neuron projection membrane, synaptic target attraction, signal transduction, pattern formation, and asymmetric cell division (Figure 1G right, for full iPAGE, GO term analysis see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by iPAGE pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1G and supplement.

claim: Blue Polycomb chromatin genes occupied by OGT were involved in GO terms such as dendrite morphogenesis, axon guidance, actin filament organization, transcription factor activity, MAPK kinase signaling, and Transforming Growth Factor β pathway.
source: These blue Polycomb chromatin genes were involved in GO terms such as dendrite morphogenesis (8.9E−08), axon guidance (7.88E−04), actin filament organization (2.45E−07), transcription factor activity (3.8E−07), MAPK kinase signaling (9.18E−05), and Transforming Growth Factor β pathway (0.0042).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis with statistical significance values provided.

claim: The epigenetic silencer PRC2.1 was necessary and sufficient to drive sweet-taste plasticity in response to the nutrient environment.
source: Our previous work showed that the epigenetic silencer PRC2.1 – specifically its H3K27m activity – was necessary and sufficient to drive sweet-taste plasticity in response to the nutrient environment (Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In the presence of high dietary sugar, PRC2.1 decreased chromatin accessibility and expression of transcription factors involved in synaptic function and signaling.
source: In the presence of high dietary sugar, PRC2.1 decreased chromatin accessibility and expression of transcription factors involved in synaptic function and signaling; these genes were located in blue-Polycomb H3K27m chromatin.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Vaziri et al., 2020).

claim: Approximately 10% of chromatin intervals were shared between Dam::Pcl and Dam::OGT.
source: A comparison of the peaks occupied by both Dam::Pcl (pink, Pcl is the recruiter for PRC2.1) and Dam::OGT (green) revealed a small number of shared intervals (Figure 2A, ~10%; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 162 loci shared by OGT and Pcl were enriched in the blue 'Polycomb' chromatin.
source: These 162 loci were enriched in the blue 'Polycomb' chromatin (p < 0.001, permutation test)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using permutation test.

claim: OGT × Pcl intervals had lower expression levels in the Gr5a+ neurons compared to those bound by OGT alone.
source: and had lower expression levels in the Gr5a+ neurons (from TRAP experiment in Vaziri et al., 2020) compared to those bound by OGT alone (Figure 2B, purple vs. green)
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 2B from TRAP experiments.

claim: There was more OGT and Pcl at the OGT × Pcl shared sites in the sugar diet condition compared to control diet.
source: There was more OGT and Pcl at the OGT × Pcl shared sites in the SD condition compared to CD, and more OGT than Pcl was present at these sites in both diets (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Dam-ID occupancy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chromatin accessibility at OGT × Pcl was markedly (50%) decreased on sugar diet compared to control diet.
source: Strikingly, chromatin accessibility at OGT × Pcl was markedly (50%) decreased on SD compared to CD (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by CaTaDA data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The nutrient-dependent shift in accessibility at OGT × Pcl loci was threefold higher than at those bound by OGT alone.
source: This nutrient-dependent shift in accessibility was threefold higher at the shared loci compared to those bound by OGT alone (compare Figures 1F and 2D; also comparatively higher than those bound by PRC2.1 alone, Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by comparison of CaTaDA data across different figures.

claim: Genes co-occupied by OGT and Pcl were enriched in regulatory pathways involved in sequence-specific DNA binding, including those implicated in neural differentiation, sodium channel regulator activity, Transforming Growth Factor β and Activin receptor signaling, and dendrite development.
source: GO term analysis of genes shared by OGT/Pcl targets revealed enrichment in regulatory pathways involved in sequence-specific DNA binding, including those implicated in neural differentiation, sodium channel regulator activity, Transforming Growth Factor β and Activin receptor signaling, and dendrite development (Figure 2E, left).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 30% of the OGT × Pcl sites corresponded to genes encoding DNA-binding and regulatory factors, including two Homeobox transcription factors known to play a role in sweet-taste function and plasticity, cad and Ptx1.
source: 30% of the OGT × Pcl sites corresponded to genes encoding DNA-binding and regulatory factors, including two Homeobox transcription factors known to play a role in sweet-taste function and plasticity, cad and Ptx1 (Figure 2E, right) (Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by analysis of gene functions and citation to previous work.

claim: Analysis of protein interactions between OGT × PRC2.1 genes uncovered a Protein–Protein Interaction network enrichment among DNA-binding factors, MAPK, signal transduction, neuron projection, and response to stimuli.
source: Analysis of protein interactions between OGT × PRC2.1 genes (Szklarczyk et al., 2020) uncovered a Protein–Protein Interaction network enrichment (p < 1.0e−16) among DNA-binding factors (pink, p = 2.08e−09), Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK, blue, p = 0.00059), signal transduction (Transforming Growth Factor, TGF-β/Activin signaling, yellow), neuron projection (red outline, p = 4.95e−7), and response to stimuli (p = 7.15e−0.5).
evidence: Supported by STRING protein interaction network analysis with statistical significance values.

claim: Knocking down OGT in the Gr5a+ sweet-sensing neurons resulted in flies with similar sweet sensitivity between control and sugar diets.
source: However, knocking down OGT in the Gr5a+ sweet-sensing neurons resulted in flies with similar sweet sensitivity between the two diets (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: OGT is required for diet-dependent sweet-taste plasticity.
source: Thus, OGT is required for diet-dependent sweet-taste plasticity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both protein null (OGT1) and catalytically dead (OGTK872M) mutants prevented the lower PER to sucrose observed in sugar diet-fed control flies.
source: Neither mutant affected sweet-taste responses on a control diet, but both prevented the lower PER to sucrose observed in SD-fed control flies (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with OGT mutants shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The catalytic activity of OGT is required for the effects of this enzyme on taste plasticity.
source: This argues that the catalytic activity of OGT is required for the effects of this enzyme on taste plasticity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with catalytically dead OGT mutant.

claim: Knocking down the antagonistic enzyme O-GlcNAcase (OGA) resulted in lower sweet-taste responses on control diet.
source: Consistent with this, knocking down the antagonistic enzyme O-GlcNAcase (OGA), which removes the GlcNAc moiety from proteins, resulted in lower sweet-taste responses on CD (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with OGA knockdown shown in Figure 3D.

claim: OGT activity is linear across all levels of cellular UDP-GlcNAc.
source: OGT activity is linear across all levels of cellular UDP-GlcNAc, so increasing its levels also increases its activity (Hart, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established knowledge about OGT biochemistry.

claim: Overexpression of OGT in the Gr5a+ neurons resulted in sucrose responses on control diet comparable to those observed in sugar diet-fed flies.
source: Overexpression of OGT in the Gr5a+ neurons resulted in sucrose responses on CD comparable to those observed in sugar diet-fed flies (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with OGT overexpression shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Inhibiting the activity of OGT with the specific OGT Small Molecule Inhibitor-1 (OSMI) blocked the effects of OGT overexpression on sweet-taste responses.
source: However, inhibiting the activity of OGT with the specific OGT Small Molecule Inhibitor-1 (OSMI) (Ortiz-Meoz et al., 2015; May et al., 2020) blocked the effects of OGT overexpression on sweet-taste responses (Figure 3E, right)
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with OSMI treatment shown in Figure 3E.

claim: OSMI treatment had no effect on survival.
source: this drug treatment had no effect on survival (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: OSMI entirely blocked the effects of sugar diet on taste plasticity.
source: Control (vehicle, Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO)) flies exhibited a dulling of sweet-taste responses on SD (squares), but this decrease was entirely blocked by OSMI (Figure 3F); no effects were observed on a CD (circles).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with OSMI treatment during diet exposure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Decreasing the activity of OGT, either with genetics or pharmacological tools, resulted in similar effects on taste plasticity.
source: Thus, decreasing the activity of OGT, either with genetics or pharmacological tools, resulted in similar effects on taste plasticity, arguing that the activity of this enzyme plays an essential role in taste changes in response to the dietary environment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments using genetic and pharmacological approaches.

claim: OSMI treatment completely abolished the changes in chromatin accessibility observed with sugar diet at OGT × Pcl sites.
source: Strikingly, OSMI treatment completely abolished the changes in chromatin accessibility observed with SD at OGT × Pcl sites (Figure 4A, compared to Figure 2D; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by CaTaDA data with OSMI treatment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OGT activity is necessary for diet-dependent dynamics at OGT × Pcl chromatin loci.
source: suggesting that OGT activity is necessary for diet-dependent dynamics at these loci.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from OSMI effects on chromatin accessibility.

claim: Inhibition of OGT activity did not affect Pcl occupancy at OGT × Pcl peaks.
source: However, inhibition of OGT activity did not affect Pcl occupancy at these peaks, indicating that recruitment of PRC2.1 to these sites is largely independent of this metabolic enzyme (pink, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Dam::Pcl occupancy data with OSMI treatment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OSMI had a mild effect on the occupancy of Dam::Pcl genomewide since the number (~1800), and identity (80%) of Dam::Pcl peaks were mainly the same with or without OSMI.
source: OSMI also had a mild effect on the occupancy of Dam::Pcl genomewide since the number (~1800), and identity (80%) of Dam::Pcl peaks were mainly the same with or without OSMI (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of Dam::Pcl peaks with and without OSMI shown in supplementary figure.

claim: OGT activity is required for the diet-dependent decrease in chromatin accessibility but not PRC2.1 recruitment or occupancy.
source: Thus, OGT activity is required for the diet-dependent decrease in chromatin accessibility but not PRC2.1 recruitment or occupancy, suggesting that other factors or events mediate these.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from OSMI effects on chromatin accessibility and Pcl occupancy.

claim: The catalytic activity of OGT was necessary for PRC2.1-mediated taste modulation.
source: However, we found that the catalytic activity of OGT was necessary for PRC2.1-mediated taste modulation.
evidence: Supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overexpression of Pcl in the Gr5a+ neurons mimics the effects of sugar diet on taste by decreasing responses to sucrose in flies fed a control diet.
source: Overexpression of Pcl in the Gr5a+ neurons mimics the effects of SD on taste by decreasing responses to sucrose in flies fed a CD (Figure 4B, left) – a result dependent on the H3K27 methylation activity of this complex (Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with Pcl overexpression and citation to previous work.

claim: OSMI blocked the effects of Pcl overexpression on sucrose responses.
source: However, OSMI blocked the effects of Pcl overexpression on sucrose responses compared to vehicle-fed flies (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with Pcl overexpression and OSMI treatment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OGT is upstream of PRC2.1 at both the molecular and behavioral levels.
source: These results place OGT upstream of PRC2.1 at both the molecular and behavioral levels.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic and pharmacological epistasis experiments.

claim: Pclc429 mutations blocked diet-induced taste plasticity on sugar diet.
source: Pclc429 mutations blocked diet-induced taste plasticity on SD (Figure 4C, pink vs. black, compare squares vs. circles)
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with Pcl mutants shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When Pclc429 mutants were combined with Gr5a>OGT, these flies failed to develop taste plasticity in response to sugar diet without any effects on control diet.
source: However, when Pclc429 mutants were combined with Gr5a>OGT, these flies failed to develop taste plasticity in response to SD without any effects on CD (Figure 4C purple).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with double manipulation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The effects of OGT act largely through PRC2.1.
source: Thus, Gr5a>OGT;Pclc429 phenocopied Pclc429 mutants (compare pink and purple), suggesting that the effects of OGT act largely through PRC2.1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from genetic epistasis experiment comparing phenotypes.

claim: Treatment with the specific inhibitor of PRC2 (EEDi) restored normal taste responses to control levels in Gr5a>OGT flies.
source: we treated Gr5a>OGT and control flies with a vehicle or the specific inhibitor of PRC2 (EEDi) while on CD (Qi et al., 2017). This manipulation restored normal taste responses to control levels in Gr5a>OGT flies (Figure 4D, compare right vs. left)
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with EEDi treatment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a strong genetic interaction between OGT and PRC2.1.
source: Together these results argue for a strong genetic interaction between OGT and PRC2.1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: OSMI treatment reverted or restored the expression of 52% of the differentially expressed genes with sugar diet/control diet change.
source: Indeed, further analyses revealed that OSMI treatment reverted (i.e., showed the opposite direction of change; q < 0.1, Wald test) or restored (practical equivalence test using a null hypothesis of a change of at least 1.5-fold and q < 0.05) the expression of 52% of the DEGs with SD/CD change (Figure 4E, gray are downregulated and red are upregulated)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis comparing gene expression changes with OSMI treatment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Most of the genes changed with OSMI treatment (367) were also similarly affected by a loss of function Pclc429 mutation.
source: and that most of the genes changed with OSMI treatment (367) were also similarly affected by a loss of function Pclc429 mutation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from OSMI and Pcl mutant experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Genes affected by both OSMI and Pcl mutation were enriched in metabolic and neural processes, such as chemical synapse transmission, synaptic target attraction, cell differentiation, glucose metabolism, and detection of chemical stimuli.
source: These genes were enriched in metabolic and neural processes, such as chemical synapse transmission, synaptic target attraction, cell differentiation, glucose metabolism, and detection of chemical stimuli (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G and supplement.

claim: The homeobox genes cad and Ptx1 and their regulons have been implicated in taste function and plasticity.
source: Notable among these were the homeobox cad and Ptx1 and their regulons, which have been implicated in taste function and plasticity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D; Vaziri et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by analysis of regulons and citation to previous work.

claim: Knockdown or overexpression of genes affected by OSMI and Pcl revealed a mild-to-moderate effect on sucrose sensation.
source: To functionally validate some of these new genes, we knocked down or overexpressed them (depending on their SD/CD log2 fold) in the Gr5a+ neurons and assayed sweet-taste function by PER (Figure 4F). This revealed a mild-to-moderate effect of these genes on sucrose sensation
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with genetic manipulations of candidate genes shown in Figure 4F.

claim: daw and Irk1 are direct targets of Pcl and OGT.
source: interestingly, daw and Irk1 are direct targets of Pcl and OGT.
evidence: Supported by Dam-ID occupancy data showing OGT and Pcl binding at these genes.

claim: OGT and PRC2.1 are in the same genetic pathway that directs diet-induced taste plasticity at the chromatin, transcriptional, and behavioral levels.
source: Together, these experiments place OGT and PRC2.1 in the same genetic pathway that directs diet-induced taste plasticity at the chromatin, transcriptional, and behavioral levels.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including chromatin, transcriptional, and behavioral data.

claim: The activity of the metabolic sensor OGT may provide the nutrient-dependent context for PRC2.1-mediated changes in chromatin accessibility.
source: They also argue that the activity of the metabolic sensor OGT may provide the nutrient-dependent context for PRC2.1-mediated changes in chromatin accessibility (but not PRC2.1 recruitment)
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results suggesting a model for OGT function.

claim: PRC2.1 may function as an effector of chromatin and transcriptional changes.
source: while PRC2.1 may instead function as an effector of these chromatin and transcriptional changes.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results suggesting a model for PRC2.1 function.

claim: The highest log2 fold enrichments in regulatory regions of OGT × Pcl and OGT × PREs loci were for Polycomb Group proteins like PhoRC and Trx-recruiter Trithorax-like (Trl), as well as transcription factors such as Stripe (Sr) and SREBP.
source: In this analysis, the highest log2 fold enrichments were for Polycomb Group proteins like PhoRC (1.018, p = 0.0099) and Trx-recruiter Trithorax-like (Trl, 1.972, p = 0.0099 and 0.803, p = 0.0099; Trx is antagonistic to PRC2.1), as well as transcription factors, such as the Zn-finger immediate early gene Stripe (Sr, homolog of activity-dependent human Early Growth Response 2, EGR2, alias Krox20), and the nutrient-sensitive factor Sterol-Responsive-Element Binding Protein (SREBP) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis with statistical significance values.

claim: Sr was the only factor that affected sweet-taste responses across low and high sucrose concentrations when overexpressed or knocked down in the Gr5a+ neurons.
source: To determine if they affected sweet taste, we measured the proboscis extension in response to sucrose when these genes were overexpressed or knocked down in the Gr5a+ neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). The only factor that affected sweet-taste responses across low and high sucrose concentrations was Sr
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral screen of candidate transcription factors shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Sr showed higher mRNA abundance in the sensory neurons of sugar diet flies.
source: which also showed higher mRNA abundance in the sensory neurons of SD-flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq expression data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Sr is a conserved transcription factor induced by neural activity via the MAPK/ERK pathway.
source: Sr is a conserved transcription factor induced by neural activity via the MAPK/ERK pathway (Chen et al., 2016; Gonzales et al., 2020; Beckmann and Wilce, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Sr function.

claim: Sr is essential for sensory nerve development and plasticity.
source: and is essential for sensory nerve development and plasticity (Murphy et al., 1989; Duclot and Kabbaj, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Sr function.

claim: The MAPK pathway is sensitive to neural activity and nutrients.
source: The MAPK pathway is sensitive to neural activity and nutrients (Robles-Flores et al., 2021; Papa et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on MAPK pathway regulation.

claim: The MAPK pathway is stimulated by mitogens, such as TGF-β/Activin signaling, which increase with high-sugar levels, eating, and neural activity in flies and mammals.
source: it is stimulated by mitogens, such as TGF-β/Activin signaling, which increase with high-sugar levels, eating, and neural activity in flies and mammals (Lavoie et al., 2020; Liu and Chen, 2022; Wilinski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on MAPK pathway stimulation.

claim: OGT × Pcl co-occupied loci were enriched in MAPK/ERK targets.
source: Of note, OGT × Pcl co-occupied loci were enriched in MAPK/ERK targets (Figure 2E, blue).
evidence: Supported by protein interaction network analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Enrichment for Sr cis-regulatory motifs was modest at OGT or Pcl-only loci but strong at genes bound by both factors.
source: Enrichment for Sr cis-regulatory motifs was modest at OGT or Pcl-only loci (l2fc = 0.196 and 0.398, respectively; p < 0.001 in both cases via an approximate permutation test) but strong at genes bound by both factors (OGT × Pcl = 0.429 and OGT × PREs = 0.976, p < 0.001, permutation test) (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis with statistical significance values shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a marked bias of Sr-binding sites around the TSS of OGT × PRC2.1 genes, with enrichment in the 500 bp window immediately preceding the TSS.
source: When we compared the distribution of Sr sites around the regulatory regions of OGT × PRC2.1 genes (either together or separately), we found a marked bias around the TSS (Figure 5B, top), with enrichment of Sr-binding sites in the 500 bp window immediately preceding the TSS.
evidence: Supported by analysis of Sr motif distribution relative to TSS shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes that OGT or PRC2.1 did not occupy were depleted for Sr-binding sites at the TSS.
source: In contrast, genes that OGT or PRC2.1 did not occupy, were depleted for Sr-binding sites at the TSS (Figure 5B, bottom).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Sr motif distribution shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sr-target genes had negative log2 fold changes on the sugar diet, and this repression was abolished by mutations in Pcl and by inhibition of OGT activity.
source: To this end, when we examined the expression of Sr-targets in the Gr5a+ neurons of flies on the two diets, we noticed that these genes had negative log2 fold changes on the sugar diet; this repression, however, was abolished by mutations in Pcl and by inhibition of OGT activity (Figure 5C, compare gray vs. pink and green, respectively)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis of Sr target gene expression shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpression of Sr resulted in lower electrophysiological responses of the gustatory neurons to sucrose.
source: Overexpression of Sr resulted in lower electrophysiological responses of the gustatory neurons to sucrose (Figure 5D, Mann–Whitney test, p = 0.001)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of Sr resulted in lower PER at both high and low sucrose concentrations.
source: as well as lower PER at both high and low sucrose concentrations (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The effect of Sr overexpression on taste was dependent on the catalytic activities of PRC2 and OGT.
source: This effect, however, was dependent on the catalytic activities of PRC2 and OGT. Indeed, overexpression of Sr in flies treated with OSMI (green) or with an inhibitor of PRC2 (pink, EEDi Vaziri et al., 2020) resulted in sucrose responses comparable to those of control flies (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with Sr overexpression and inhibitor treatments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Sr plays a role in taste plasticity in coordination with OGT and PRC2.1.
source: Overall, these results argue for a role of Sr in taste plasticity in coordination with OGT and PRC2.1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing functional interactions between Sr, OGT, and PRC2.1.

claim: Coordination between Sr and OGT/PRC2.1 may arise not from direct interactions but rather from two distinct paths of information flow, such as metabolism and neural activity.
source: Importantly, since OGT and PRC2.1 are not always found at TSS, the bias in Sr distribution at the TSS of 'OGT/PRC2.1 regulated genes' indicates that coordination between Sr and OGT/PRC2.1 may arise not from direct interactions but rather from two distinct paths of information flow, such as metabolism and neural activity.
evidence: Interpretation of the spatial distribution patterns of OGT, PRC2.1, and Sr binding sites.

claim: The mRNA abundance of rl (rolled/ERK) was higher in the Gr5a+ neurons of flies on sugar diet.
source: First, we observed that, as with Sr, the mRNA abundance of rl was higher in the Gr5a+ neurons of flies on SD, but this gene was not a direct target of OGT or PRC2.1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq expression data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: rl (rolled/ERK) was not a direct target of OGT or PRC2.1.
source: First, we observed that, as with Sr, the mRNA abundance of rl was higher in the Gr5a+ neurons of flies on SD, but this gene was not a direct target of OGT or PRC2.1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Dam-ID occupancy data showing no OGT or Pcl binding at rl gene.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type rl (rlWT) with Gr5a-GAL4 did not affect the electrophysiological responses of the sensory neurons to sucrose.
source: Overexpression of rlWT with Gr5a-GAL4 did not affect the electrophysiological responses of the sensory neurons to sucrose (Figure 6C, dark blue)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of constitutively active rl (rlSem) decreased neuronal responses to sucrose.
source: however, expression of the active rlSem decreased neuronal responses to sucrose (Figure 6C, light blue).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: rlWT flies had identical PER to sucrose as controls while rlSem showed reduced PER across high and low sucrose concentrations.
source: These activity phenotypes were reflected in the behavioral taste responses to sucrose, with rlWT flies having identical PER to sucrose as controls and rlSem showing reduced PER across high and low sucrose concentrations (Figure 6D, left vs. right; note that controls are shared here, plotted separately for clarity).
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: rl (rolled/ERK) activity, but not higher levels alone, was sufficient to affect sweet-taste plasticity.
source: Thus, rl activity, but not higher levels alone, was sufficient to affect sweet-taste plasticity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of rlWT and rlSem overexpression effects.

claim: rl (rolled/ERK) is necessary for sweet-taste responses, as loss of function mutants and RNAi for rl had lower electrophysiological and behavioral responses to sucrose.
source: Not surprisingly, given the known function of rl/ERK in neural activity, we found that this kinase was also necessary for sweet-taste responses, as loss of function mutants and RNAi for rl had lower electrophysiological and behavioral responses to sucrose (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology and PER data with rl mutants and RNAi shown in supplementary figure.

claim: OSMI treatment almost entirely blocked the effects of rlSem on both neural and behavioral responses to sucrose while having no effect on rlWT flies.
source: Strikingly, OSMI treatment almost entirely blocked the effects of rlSem on both neural and behavioral responses to sucrose while having no effect on rlWT flies (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology and PER data with rlSem and OSMI treatment shown in Figure 6E, F.

claim: Trametinib at 15.6 μM blocked the effects of rlSem expression on sweet-taste responses.
source: At concentrations previously used in flies (15.6 μM) (Castillo-Quan et al., 2019; Slack et al., 2015), Trametinib blocked the effects of rlSem expression on sweet-taste responses (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with Trametinib treatment shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Trametinib had no effect on survival.
source: this had no effect on survival (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Treatment with Trametinib negated the effects of Sr overexpression on sucrose responses, resulting in flies with PER comparable to controls.
source: Treatment with this ERK inhibitor also negated the effects of Sr overexpression on sucrose responses, resulting in flies with PER comparable to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), placing Sr downstream of ERK activation.
evidence: Supported by PER behavioral data with Sr overexpression and Trametinib treatment shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Sr is downstream of ERK activation.
source: Treatment with this ERK inhibitor also negated the effects of Sr overexpression on sucrose responses, resulting in flies with PER comparable to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), placing Sr downstream of ERK activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from Trametinib effects on Sr overexpression phenotype.

claim: Exposure to a high-sugar diet decreased the electrophysiological and behavioral responses to sucrose.
source: Exposure to a high-sugar diet decreased the electrophysiological (Figure 7A) and behavioral (Figure 7B) responses to sucrose.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology and PER data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: When rl activity was blocked with Trametinib, there was no decrease in neural responses or PER with sugar diet.
source: However, when rl activity was blocked with Trametinib, there was no decrease in neural responses or PER (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology and PER data with Trametinib treatment during diet exposure shown in Figure 7C, D.

claim: Trametinib had a minor but significant effect on sweet-taste activity on control diet.
source: Of note, Trametinib had a minor but significant effect on sweet-taste activity (compare CD of Figure 7C with CD of Figure 7A), consistent with the observation that rl is necessary for normal sweet-taste function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of electrophysiology data across figures.

claim: The ERK pathway plays a critical role in the development of taste adaptations in response to diet.
source: Together, these data indicate that the ERK pathway plays a critical role in the development of taste adaptations in response to diet and place its function upstream of OGT.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments with ERK pathway manipulations.

claim: The ERK pathway functions upstream of OGT in taste plasticity.
source: Together, these data indicate that the ERK pathway plays a critical role in the development of taste adaptations in response to diet and place its function upstream of OGT.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from epistasis experiments showing ERK inhibition blocks OGT-dependent effects.

claim: OGT is a conserved enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of UDP-GlcNAc to the serine and threonine residues of proteins.
source: OGT is a conserved enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of UDP-GlcNAc to the serine and threonine residues of proteins (Hart, 2019; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established knowledge about OGT biochemistry.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc synthesis by the HBP combines sugar, amino acid, nucleotide, and fatty acid metabolism.
source: Because UDP-GlcNAc synthesis by the HBP combines sugar, amino acid, nucleotide, and fatty acid metabolism, the levels of this metabolite, as well as the activity of the enzymes in this pathway, are inextricably linked to cellular metabolism and diet (Hart, 2019; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established knowledge about HBP metabolism.

claim: Higher HBP flux directly impacts OGT activity because the function of this enzyme is linear across a vast range of physiological UDP-GlcNAc concentrations.
source: Higher HBP flux directly impacts OGT activity because the function of this enzyme is linear across a vast range of physiological UDP-GlcNAc concentrations.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about OGT kinetics.

claim: OGT is recognized as a critical nutrient sensor in animal physiology, particularly in development, cancer, and metabolic disease.
source: Because of this, OGT is recognized as a critical nutrient sensor in animal physiology, particularly in development, cancer, and metabolic disease (Hart, 2019; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles on OGT function.

claim: OGT has been implicated in synapse maturation, neural excitability, activity, and plasticity.
source: More recently, its importance for neural function and plasticity has also been recognized, with studies implicating it in synapse maturation, neural excitability, activity, and plasticity (Butler et al., 2019; Ardiel et al., 2018; Lagerlöf et al., 2016; Su and Schwarz, 2017; Giles et al., 2019; Lagerlöf et al., 2017; Ruan et al., 2014; Hwang and Rhim, 2019; Li et al., 2019; May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on OGT in neural function.

claim: A high-sugar diet acutely and chronically increased HBP activity in flies.
source: Our group showed that a high-sugar diet acutely and chronically increased HPB activity in flies and played a role in diet-induced sensory plasticity (Wilinski et al., 2019; May et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The GlcNAc modification is enriched in nuclear and synaptic proteins.
source: OGT is a nucleocytoplasmic enzyme, and the GlcNAc modification is enriched in nuclear and synaptic proteins, which extends its reach on cellular physiology (Hart, 2019; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established knowledge about O-GlcNAc modification.

claim: Only one study has shown OGT's direct association with chromatin in murine embryonic stem cells prior to this work.
source: Although OGT is thought to play a role in gene regulation, only one study has shown its direct association with chromatin in murine embryonic stem cells (Vella et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to the only previous study showing OGT chromatin association.

claim: This is the first study to show that OGT-associated chromatin is nutrient sensitive.
source: This is the first study to show that OGT-associated chromatin is nutrient sensitive to the best of our knowledge.
evidence: Authors' assessment of novelty based on literature review.

claim: The H3K27 methylation activity of PRC2.1 is required for changes in chromatin accessibility, including those that depend on diet in the sensory neurons.
source: The H3K27 methylation activity of PRC2.1 is required for changes in chromatin accessibility, including those that depend on diet in the sensory neurons (Schuettengruber et al., 2017; Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies including authors' own work.

claim: OGT activity affects the repressive action but not the recruitment of PRC2.1.
source: Thus, our data suggest that OGT activity affects the repressive action but not the recruitment of PRC2.1
evidence: Conclusion drawn from OSMI effects on chromatin accessibility and Pcl occupancy.

claim: The catalytic activity of PRC2.1 is required for the effects of OGT on taste plasticity.
source: we also demonstrate that the catalytic activity of PRC2.1 is required for the effects of OGT on taste plasticity.
evidence: Supported by experiments with PRC2 inhibitor EEDi shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Several studies have linked OGT activity with the stability, chromatin occupancy, or catalytic function of Polycomb Group Proteins.
source: Several studies have linked OGT activity with the stability, chromatin occupancy, or catalytic function of Polycomb Group Proteins (Hart, 2019; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017; Chu et al., 2014; Sakabe and Hart, 2010; Forma et al., 2018; Sui et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2019; You et al., 2021; Decourcelle et al., 2020; Gambetta and Müller, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on OGT-PcG interactions.

claim: Connections between OGT and ERK have been uncovered in the context of cancer and cell division, with studies showing that inhibition of ERK signaling decreases O-GlcNAcylation and vice versa.
source: Connections between OGT and ERK have also been uncovered in the context of cancer and cell division, with studies showing that inhibition of ERK signaling decreases O-GlcNAcylation and vice versa (Zhang et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on OGT-ERK interactions.

claim: GlcNAcylation promotes ERK effects while OGT inhibition blocks them.
source: and that GlcNAcylation promotes ERK effects while OGT inhibition blocks them (Cork et al., 2018; Weiss et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on OGT-ERK functional interactions.

claim: OGT could affect chromatin accessibility by GlcNAcylating histones, although the function and effects of these histone modifications are still poorly understood.
source: OGT could also affect chromatin accessibility by GlcNAcylating histones, although the function and effects of these histone modifications are still poorly understood (Gambetta and Müller, 2015; Hirosawa et al., 2018; Konzman et al., 2020; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanisms supported by citations to studies on histone O-GlcNAcylation.

claim: In the sweet-taste neurons, sugar directly activates the cells via receptor-dependent mechanisms and enhances OGT's metabolic activity.
source: In the case of the sweet-taste neurons, sugar directly activates the cells via receptor-dependent mechanisms and enhances OGT's metabolic activity.
evidence: Based on known mechanisms of sweet taste reception and OGT regulation by sugar metabolism.

claim: Integrating metabolic and activity signals at the level of chromatin is key for developing sensory plasticity.
source: Our data support the idea that integrating these two signals at the level of chromatin – a synergy almost entirely unique to these cells – is key for developing sensory plasticity.
evidence: Interpretation of the collective experimental findings.

claim: The activity-dependent ERK pathway provides a relevant cellular context (likely neural activity) for adaptations to the nutrient environment.
source: Together, these molecular and functional data support the idea that the activity-dependent ERK pathway provides a relevant cellular context (likely neural activity) for adaptations to the nutrient environment.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results on ERK pathway function.

claim: PRC2.1 likely plays the role of effector in nutrigenomic signaling since the effects of ERK/EGR2 and OGT manipulations were dependent on PRC2.1 function.
source: However, these sensing mechanisms must be turned into action to be effective. This is likely the role of PRC2.1 since the effects of ERK/EGR2 and OGT manipulations were dependent on the PRC2.1 function.
evidence: Interpretation of genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Only a small portion of the genes occupied by PRC2.1 is sensitive to diet and OGT activity.
source: Of note, only a small portion of the genes occupied by PRC2.1 is sensitive to diet and OGT activity, and our data show that PRC2.1 is not binding to new loci but instead tuning the output of those it is already bound to, likely via OGT instruction.
evidence: Supported by comparison of PRC2.1 occupancy with and without OSMI and diet changes.

claim: The 162 co-occupied loci identified were enriched for transcription and regulatory factors involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, signaling, and neural activity, as well as pathways implicated in neural plasticity.
source: The 162 co-occupied loci identified were enriched for transcription and regulatory factors involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, signaling, and neural activity, as well as pathways implicated in neural plasticity.
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis of OGT × Pcl genes.

claim: Many DNA-binding factors at OGT × Pcl loci play essential roles during the development of sensory neurons to set their biophysical properties, such as Ptx1 and cad, but also affect adult taste plasticity.
source: Many of these DNA-binding factors play essential roles during the development of sensory neurons to set their biophysical properties, such as Ptx1 and cad, but also affect adult taste plasticity.
evidence: Supported by previous studies on these transcription factors and current behavioral data.

claim: The regulons of transcription factors at OGT × Pcl loci include genes known to affect pre- and postsynaptic branching and structure, as well as synaptic physiology.
source: The regulons of these TFs include genes known to affect pre- and postsynaptic branching and structure, as well as synaptic physiology.
evidence: Supported by analysis of transcription factor regulons and their functions.

claim: This nutrigenomic pathway promotes taste adaptations, most likely by re-engaging developmental gene batteries, a mechanism that has been hypothesized to play a role in neural plasticity.
source: Thus, our collective data indicate that this nutrigenomic pathway promotes taste adaptations, most likely by re-engaging developmental gene batteries, a mechanism that has been hypothesized to play a role in neural plasticity (Hobert, 2011; Marder and Prinz, 2002; Parrish et al., 2014; Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citations to previous hypotheses about neural plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Many neural and psychiatric conditions show associations and connections with diet and metabolic states, including epilepsy, schizophrenia, bipolar, depression, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's.
source: On this note, many neural and psychiatric conditions show associations and connections with diet and metabolic states, including epilepsy, schizophrenia, bipolar, depression, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's (Sarangi and Dus, 2021; Grigolon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles on diet-brain connections.

claim: Uncovering nutrigenomic mechanisms in the brain could shed light on the etiology of neural and psychiatric conditions and help design nutritional strategies to support people suffering from them.
source: Thus, uncovering nutrigenomic mechanisms in the brain could shed light on the etiology of these conditions and help design nutritional strategies to support people suffering from them; this is similar to how metabolic disorders like diabetes and cardiovascular disease are treated with a combination of drugs and nutrition.
evidence: Speculation about potential applications of the research findings.

claim: Cell and context specificity transforms 'nutritional data' into nutritional information.
source: More generally, we put forth a model where cell and context specificity transforms 'nutritional data' – that is, variations in nutrient and metabolite levels – into nutritional information (Floridi, 2005), as shown in Figure 7E (pink boxes).
evidence: Conceptual model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Nutrigenomic mechanisms could provide a critical path for information flow in biological systems.
source: Thus, nutrigenomic mechanisms could provide a critical path for information flow in biological systems (Shannon, 1948; Reinagel, 2000; Smith, 2000; Fabris, 2009).
evidence: Speculation about broader implications supported by citations to information theory.

claim: A clear advantage of nutrigenomic mechanisms could reside in their ability to amplify transient, and often minor, variations in nutrient and activity levels into strong reactions.
source: A clear advantage could reside in their ability to amplify transient, and often minor, variations in nutrient and activity levels into strong reactions, which can be used to orchestrate responses to current and future environmental challenges.
evidence: Speculation about the functional significance of nutrigenomic signaling.
